analysis.one_liner: Ends the overtime pay exemption for long-haul truck drivers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 6 senators, was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended, so truck drivers still have no federal right to overtime pay.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike a line in federal labor law that exempts motor carrier (truck) employees from overtime pay rules. That change would require trucking employers to pay drivers time-and-a-half for hours worked beyond 40 a week, like most other workers. The bill was introduced in November 2023, sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Truck drivers, who are currently exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act's overtime rules. Many are paid by the mile rather than by the hour and routinely work long weeks, so hours over 40 often bring no premium pay. Repealing the exemption would entitle them to time-and-a-half for those hours, raising pay for the longest-working drivers and adding a financial cost to employers for keeping drivers on duty excessively long hours.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the provision that exempts motor carrier employees from federal overtime pay requirements, putting truck drivers under the same overtime rules as most other workers.

Truckers would gain the right to overtime at 1.5 times their regular rate for hours beyond 40 per week. Because many drivers are paid per mile and work 60- to 70-hour weeks, the change targets a workforce where long hours are the norm and unpaid or underpaid waiting and loading time is common.

By making hours past 40 substantially more expensive for employers, the bill would give trucking companies a direct financial reason to schedule more reasonable hours, which relates to the widely documented fatigue problems in long-haul trucking.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and motor carriers, who would owe overtime premiums for hours over 40. Those with thin margins — particularly small carriers — would bear the largest adjustment, and some of the added labor cost would likely be passed along in freight rates to shippers and, eventually, consumer prices.

drawbacks.text: The direct cost falls on motor carriers, and freight rates would likely rise as companies passed higher labor costs to shippers and consumers, a real cost at a time when freight prices affect the price of nearly everything shipped by truck.

Truck drivers' hours are already capped by federal hours-of-service rules rather than the 40-hour week that governs overtime for most workers. Critics have long argued that the overtime exemption is unnecessary because safety rules, not pay incentives, are the binding limit on driver hours, and that trucking operates on thin margins where new labor costs could push small carriers out of business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a concrete wage gain for a large workforce that is currently one of the biggest groups excluded from overtime law, and a built-in price signal against extreme hours. The cost is higher freight labor expenses, some of which reach consumers through shipping prices. The bill is a single-sentence repeal, so it is simple to administer, but it pairs the wage gain with no transitional help for small carriers, meaning the smallest operators would feel the squeeze first.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, sent to the labor committee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress expired in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Alex Padilla introduced the bill on November 9, 2023, joined by five colleagues: Senators Markey, Sanders, Warren, Blumenthal, and Wyden.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. That referral was its only action.
The committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill. It died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies and motor carriers are better off, because the current law that lets them avoid overtime premiums for hours over 40 stays on the books. Drivers who work long weeks are worse off, having gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking companies that avoided overtime costs

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Markey, Sanders, Warren, Blumenthal, and Wyden
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill six Senate sponsors in total.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after receiving the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote. The referral on November 9, 2023 was the bill's only recorded action.

against.name: Trucking industry groups
against.what_they_did: Industry groups representing motor carriers have long opposed extending overtime pay requirements to truck drivers, arguing that federal hours-of-service safety limits already cap driver hours and that new overtime costs would strain thin-margin carriers.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent (Sanders); no Republican cosponsored, and there was never a roll-call vote because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill's only substantive effect is to end the exemption these companies rely on under Section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, requiring them to pay time-and-a-half for hours over 40. Their current pay-by-the-mile model, in which long hours carry no premium, is precisely what the bill would upend.

These shippers buy trucking services and would likely see some of the higher labor cost passed through in freight rates. They also share an interest in carriers operating sustainably rather than relying on exhausted drivers.
